rv.q: “A Wonderful World: The Louis Armstrong Musical” is a majestic spectacle, paying homage to a towering figure and his distinctive legacy.
What we’re seeing on stage is too entertaining.

To showcase and to dissect always are tricky, twin ambitions for any jukebox show, and I think the main problem with “Wonderful World” is that it worries too much about the latter, which gets in the way of fully delivering the former.
In the case of A Wonderful World, Louis Armstrong comes marching into Broadway aboard an overstuffed bio-musical.
The musical offers a pleasing depiction of that joy and that mask, if not of those multitudes.

Iglehart is aptly charming in this role — the modulations and mimicry of that iconic gravel is everything you want it to be — but charisma alone can only do so much to invigorate a plain script that too often skims over the complexities of Louis’ life as a Black artist in the early 20th century.
What’s on Broadway is largely a deflating and cobbled-together wife story that fails to capture Armstrong, the artist.

“A Wonderful World,” treating its title as purely ironic, does not sufficiently encompass that complexity; it’s vague because it cannot reconcile Armstrong’s overflowing affections (for women, music and people of all stripes) with the rigid absolutes of our time.
A Wonderful World refuses to look away from the racism that latched its claws into Armstrong's career... keeping A Wonderful World lively and interesting.

As bio-musicals go, A Wonderful World doesn't break any new ground, and the book by Aurin Squire is pretty much by-the-numbers, hitting most of the highs and lows spanning 70 years in Armstrong's storied career.

Iglehart winningly embodies a well-loved national figure, and A Wonderful World, directed by Christopher Renshaw and co-directed by Iglehart and Christina Sajous, benefits mightily from this, telling a story that, as a matter of the facts told, wasn’t all toothy smiles.
Indeed, for all of its considerable entertainment value, “A Wonderful World” makes it hard for us to fully invest in Armstrong and the many people in his life.
The effort to do both does no particular favor to either.
Maybe that's too much for one show to bear.
But have we gotten to know Armstrong as a musician, husband, cultural force, his politics, his passion for music, his strengths and frailties?
But oddly, the wattage of his wives dims the light on Armstrong himself.
The disappointing new biomusical A Wonderful World: The Louis Armstrong Musical suffers from a frustrating case of split identity.
Alas, as depicted in “A Wonderful World,” the late jazz giant comes across as puzzlingly smaller than life, or smaller than Armstrong’s life, at least.
But when you try to tell everything, nothing means much of anything; characters and incidents come and go in rapid succession, rarely making an impact.
Mostly, I wished that Teachout’s play, which is more emotional, nuanced, and satisfying, had been granted the bright lights of Broadway, not a potato sack like this.

To say the least, it’s a lackluster concluding statement on the complexities of Armstrong’s marriages, as well as his feelings about a world that, despite all of its “trees of green” and “red roses too,” caused him so much pain.
As presented here, Armstrong is a talented and very amiable man whose only real direction in life is collecting a lot of wives, each of whom gets about 30 minutes on stage.
Don’t miss being a part of it at Studio 54.
You’ll leave the theater acknowledging that this is, indeed, a wonderful world.
Christopher Renshaw helms the best musical entertainment on Broadway thus far this season—and likely beyond.
Ultimately, this musical is a moving tribute to Armstrong’s legacy, blending his triumphs, challenges, and the infectious joy of his music into an unforgettable theatrical experience.

A Wonderful World is an important story, a hopeful story with a sunny disposition, a story that believes in the possibility of change and in seeing the beauty in the world and trying to build a better one – with music and with love.
Overall, A Wonderful World was a miraculous production full of genuine smiles for audience and cast alike; despite brief moments of darkness, the show filled our hearts with light and spirit.
This intentional shift from trauma to a celebration of his music and cultural impact makes for an entertaining, though not groundbreaking, night at the theater.
Those unexpected and rage-fueled moments (as well as Alphonso Horne's expert trumpeting) lifted the rest of this mostly standard bio-musical.
A Wonderful World doesn’t offer a very deep understanding of Louis Armstrong and what made him a legend, but less can still be Satchmo.
Somehow, though, Armstrong should be a big presence and figuratively should take up the entire theater.
This play is a great recreation of his music with terrific dancing, but it’s more vaudeville show than drama.
The formula is not as unique as his brand of music is, and unfortunately for this biographical musical, the only excitement that exists is in the supreme talent displayed on stage...
So A Wonderful World isn't a bad show.
In view of what's happening outside, the wonderful world on stage at Studio 54 does just fine.

cn.t: Critics find Iglehart's Armstrong portrayal electrifying, but the book draws fire for being formulaic and surface-level. A musically rich but dramatically thin jukebox bio.

vs.sum: The legendary former nightclub retains a distinctive atmosphere even in its theatrical configuration. However, comfort is among the worst on Broadway — the rear mezzanine is extremely steep with limited guardrails and tight legroom throughout both levels.

acc.note: No elevator to Mezzanine. 10 induction loops. 81 assistive listening devices. Orchestra wheelchair seating.

vr.q: I was surprised by how much I enjoyed this on Broadway
I don't know if I'd consider this a must-see, but unless you really dislike jazz music for some strange reason, you'll definitely find something to enjoy here.
if you want to see just a great performance by everyone in general including James Monroe eagleheart as Louis Armstrong go check the show out
A wonderful world is ultimately not doing anything to break the mold, but it fits the mold very well. And if you like that kind of musical, you're going to enjoy this.
